newsitem.title: USA: Consumers seek new U.S. electric merger standards.
newsitem.headline: Consumers seek new U.S. electric merger standards.

text.p: Several groups came together Tuesday pressing Congress to toughen electric utility merger standards to protect consumers from mega-utilities which could charge steep rates in a deregulated power market.
The coalition of consumer advocates and public power utilities, Consumers for Fair Competition, includes groups with diverging goals in the debate over opening power markets to competition.
But they agree they do not want to see investor-owned utilities gearing up for competition by merging with each other, getting rid of potential rivals in the evolving market.
"Unless the concentration of control in the electric industry is reduced, competition will fail and consumers will not benefit," the coalition said in a letter to lawmakers.

It urged Congress to direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to reject or impose conditions on any merger, including gas and electric mergers, that would create a dominant company in any area, or product or service market.
It also urged Congress to give the FERC authority to protect ratepayers from subsidizing utilities' efforts to move into other businesses, if Congress repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act.
In line with a recommendation by the FERC, the coalition said Congress should give the commission the authority to police transmission on the power grid to ensure that power supplies remain reliable.

The FERC should also be ordered to require transmission owners to hand over control of their facilities to independent operators, so that no single utility can keep competing power providers off their systems, the coalition said.

Charles Higley, senior analyst for the consumer group Public Citizen, said the best way to create a fair market would be to make power plant owners sell off their transmission and distribution assets.
"Divestiture is the only way we can try to reduce the amount of regulation and protect consumers," he said at a news conference.

The groups said the FERC should find a new way to price electricity transmission so that it reflects the actual flow of electrons through the grid and avoids layering of rates by utilities along an imaginary flow path set in contracts.
